CHIEF COMPLAINT
Chest pain with referral from emergency room for evaluation of esophagitis.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a new patient referred from the ER three months ago with a complaint of chest pain that occurred in early October 2020. She reports that the chest pain started randomly and lasted for four days. The pain was sharp, substernal in location, and felt like a heart attack. She was unable to relieve it with any interventions and went to the emergency room on the fourth day. In the ER, she underwent an EKG and blood tests, which were all normal. She also reported associated difficulty swallowing during this episode. The chest pain and dysphagia resolved approximately three days after the ER visit. Since that time, she has remained asymptomatic for three months. She denies heartburn but acknowledges that the chest pain worsened with eating. She reports that she was going through a stressful job transition at the time of the symptom onset. She notes that she wanted to see a physician three months ago but this was the first available appointment.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for chest pain (now resolved), dysphagia (now resolved), and upper abdominal discomfort. Negative for lower abdominal pain. Bowel movements are normal. Denies any abdominal pain currently.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Uterine fibroids
Anemia
Cholecystectomy several years ago

MEDICATIONS
Not documented.

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient denies family history of GI problems.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient reports she has been trying to lose weight.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Abdomen: Soft. Lower abdomen nontender. Mild tenderness to light palpation in the upper abdominal quadrants, symmetric on left and right. No acute distress noted.

RESULTS
ER workup included normal cardiac evaluation, normal EKG, and normal blood tests.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Chest pain, resolved. Differential diagnosis includes GERD, dyspepsia, esophagitis, musculoskeletal etiologies, and anxiety. Most likely etiology is anxiety related to job transition at the time of symptom onset, with possible contribution from musculoskeletal causes. Given that the patient has been asymptomatic for three months, an EGD is unlikely to reveal active esophagitis at this time. Patient and physician discussed options of EGD versus continued monitoring for symptoms. Patient elected to self-monitor her symptoms and will call the office if she experiences any recurrence of chest pain, additional episodes, or any other concerning symptoms. If symptoms recur, EGD will be scheduled. She will follow up with me as needed for any other GI complaints.
